newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Netanyahu vows to make peace -- with Levy.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Netanyahu vows to make peace -- with Levy.

text.p: Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu tried to calm Foreign Minister David Levy on Tuesday by offering him day-to-day control over peacemaking with the Palestinians.
On Monday Levy, 59, threatened to quit over the way the prime minister runs the government in a move that edged the fractious coalition closer to a precipice.
A veteran of political brinkmanship, Levy accused Netanyahu of keeping him in the dark on important issues including political appointments and peace moves.
"I intend to meet the foreign minister and determine with him the suitable arrangements for the government's work," Netanyahu, 47, told reporters in Ramat Gan near Tel Aviv.

"I believe the most natural thing from my standpoint is that the foreign minister guide the daily work between us and the Palestinians," he said. "I believe a way will be found also to implement this."

No one expected Levy's quarrel with Netanyahu to bring down the government soon, but the threat underscored growing disenchantment with the prime minister and with a 3-1/2-month-old crisis in peacemaking over Jewish settlement construction.
A poll published on Monday showed that three-quarters of Israelis want a change in government.
"Most of the cabinet ministers also understand that the national sport of beating on the government and the prime minister isn't good for them," said Netanyahu, leader of the right-wing Likud party.
A media disclosure on Friday that National Infrastructure Minister Ariel Sharon had secretly met top PLO official Mahmoud Abbas triggered Levy's threat to resign.
"The question is, whether as foreign minister I should know things after the fact," Levy told reporters on Monday.
He said his Gesher faction, with five of the 66 coalition seats in the 120-member parliament, had been disappointed by Netanyahu's failure to advance peace or to improve life for low-income Israelis.
If Levy took Gesher out of the government, Netanyahu's fate would depend on an unstable parliamentary majority of one built on rebellious Likud members threatening to bolt.
Two ministers have already quit the cabinet. Netanyahu had hoped to get parliamentary approval on Monday for Sharon to replace one of them, Dan Meridor, as finance minister.
But Levy balked at Sharon's demand to join Levy, the prime minister and Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai in an inner cabinet team that shapes peace policy.
Instead, Levy said, the so-called "kitchen cabinet" should be scrapped and important decisions made by the full cabinet.

Public Security Minister Avigdor Kahalani, leader of the right-centre Third Way party in the coalition, was taking no chances. He said his four-member faction was preparing for the possibility of elections.
